question_text: Assess the effectiveness of the options available to organic and biodynamic grape growers to control pests and diseases.
command_word_demand: "Far too many papers described, but did not assess the options as the paper requires." The examiners state the verb demanded analysis of trade-offs, not enumeration: "The question required the use of analytical skills to address fundamental decisions vital to grape growers with more limited resources relative to conventional growers."

definitions_required.quote: Most did not define 'effectiveness', particularly the economic/financial implications.

required_elements.element: Define 'effectiveness', explicitly including the economic/financial implications of each control option
required_elements.quote: Most did not define 'effectiveness', particularly the economic/financial implications.

required_elements.element: Assess (weigh up) the options rather than describe them
required_elements.quote: Far too many papers described, but did not assess the options as the paper requires.

required_elements.element: Distinguish organic from biodynamic conceptually (containment vs prevention)
required_elements.quote: Nor were there many papers that clearly understood the conceptual differences between organic and biodynamic options (containment vs. prevention).

required_elements.element: Make examples clearly attributable to organic OR biodynamic practice, not blurred together
required_elements.quote: In too many instances, examples did not distinguish between organic and biodynamic.

required_elements.element: Frame the analysis around the fundamental decisions facing growers with more limited resources than conventional growers
required_elements.quote: The question required the use of analytical skills to address fundamental decisions vital to grape growers with more limited resources relative to conventional growers.

required_elements.element: Cover control through canopy management, not only sprays and predator habitat
required_elements.quote: While many papers successfully discussed pest and disease control treatments using copper or sulphur, and habitat for predator animals, too few dealt with control through canopy management.

credit_signals.signal: Competent treatment of copper/sulphur treatments and habitat for predator animals
credit_signals.quote: While many papers successfully discussed pest and disease control treatments using copper or sulphur, and habitat for predator animals, too few dealt with control through canopy management.

penalty_signals.signal: Answer reads as a catalogue of pests/diseases and their remedies
penalty_signals.quote: Quoting one Examiner: "This essay reads like a list of pests/diseases and measures growers use to address them."

penalty_signals.signal: Presenting mainstream sustainable/conventional techniques as uniquely organic
penalty_signals.quote: Some papers treated some means of control as uniquely organic, such as pheromone usage and raptor control, when in fact these are now standard practices under sustainable and even many conventional growing systems.

penalty_signals.signal: No definition of 'effectiveness', so no yardstick against which to assess
penalty_signals.quote: Most did not define 'effectiveness', particularly the economic/financial implications.

penalty_signals.signal: Omitting canopy management as a control lever
penalty_signals.quote: too few dealt with control through canopy management.

examples_expected.specificity: Examples must be clearly identified as organic or biodynamic; the Panel Chair's paper-level comment adds that generic examples are inadequate.
examples_expected.quote: In too many instances, examples did not distinguish between organic and biodynamic.

performance_note: "This question was answered by only one third of the candidates, and overall, not very successfully."
extraction_notes: The items in named_in_report are control TECHNIQUES the commentary names, not places or producers — the report names no regional or producer examples for this question. Note that 'pheromone usage' and 'raptor control' are named only to be criticised as NOT uniquely organic; a grader should not credit them as organic-specific. Paper-level preamble (Joel Butler MW) also applies: papers failed by not providing definitions where required, not answering both parts, factual inaccuracy, and answering "too generally and with inadequate generic examples"; "Reciting arguments from viticulture textbooks, while perhaps correct, will not suffice."

question_text: What practical options does a viticulturist have at his or her disposal to address long term changes in climate in an established vineyard?

command_word_demand: The examiners treat the question as demanding practical options set inside a defined long-term horizon and inside an existing vineyard: "Absolutely critical to success here was defining 'Long Term' and also noting the answer had to be about an established vineyard. command_word_demand: The examiners read the stem as a four-part instruction and marked against all four: "Good answers realised and responded to the four parts of the question: WHEN / HOW / PREVENTION / RESPONSE." The final part demands evaluation, not listing: "followed by an assessment of potential means of prevention or response to damage."

extraction_notes: Musar, Beaucastel and Grange are deliberately NOT in named_in_report: the report names them only as over-used and dated, so a grader must not treat citing them as a credit signal. The commentary opens with a 'Key Understanding' block (the examiners' pre-stated expectation) followed by post-hoc performance commentary; both are report text and both were mined. A page number ('the key 9 purveyors') was removed from one quote.

question_text: Shape, size and material of a vessel used for fermentation and maturation are important factors in determining style and quality. Discuss with particular reference to Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay.
command_word_demand: Discussion here meant causal analysis, not a survey of practice: "Candidates should not merely have discussed who does what but should have analysed the important factors that determine quality and style." And: "Strong answers must address the physical dynamics of why certain shapes / sizes / materials have a material effect upon end flavours."

required_elements.element: Address BOTH named varieties — declining one forfeits marks
required_elements.quote: Many candidates asserted their right to speak only of either Chardonnay or Cabernet Sauvignon and consequently limited their scope for gaining marks… when the question specifies the varietal commentary required, it is not sufficient for a candidate to state in their introduction that they do not intend to address one or other of the named varieties.

required_elements.element: Discuss both fermentation and maturation
required_elements.quote: They must discuss both fermentation and maturation.

required_elements.element: Explain the physical dynamics by which shape/size/material change the end flavour
required_elements.quote: Strong answers must address the physical dynamics of why certain shapes / sizes / materials have a material effect upon end flavours.

required_elements.element: Show that some of these choices are highly grape-variety specific
required_elements.quote: They should make it clear that these choices are sometimes highly grape variety specific.

required_elements.element: Show global breadth of styles and qualities from both varieties, across classic and non-classic origins
required_elements.quote: Candidates must be able to show depth and breadth of knowledge about which styles and qualities are produced from these two varieties globally and consider styles with reference to classic / non classic origins.

required_elements.element: Analyse the determinants of style and quality rather than catalogue who does what
required_elements.quote: Candidates should not merely have discussed who does what but should have analysed the important factors that determine quality and style.

required_elements.element: Cover the full market, not only premium wines
required_elements.quote: Again, Examiners noted that candidates focussed too heavily on the premium end of the market. The best candidates covered the use of various vessels for both wine types and a range of styles.

credit_signals.signal: Grasping the full range of options while staying practically realistic
credit_signals.quote: Candidates that performed well grasped the dimensions of possibility whilst maintaining a grip upon practicality.

credit_signals.signal: Acknowledging excellent wines made in unfashionable vessels
credit_signals.quote: They also tended to acknowledge the fact that there are many wineries making excellent wines from vessels and materials that are not currently in vogue - so a palpable sense of practical realism helped strengthen their arguments.

credit_signals.signal: Presenting a clear spectrum of causes and effects
credit_signals.quote: Recognition of the fact that different vessel materials and shapes and sizes do make significant differences to wine style was crucial and the best papers presented a spectrum of clearly stated causes and effects.

credit_signals.signal: Covering various vessels across both varieties and a range of styles
credit_signals.quote: The best candidates covered the use of various vessels for both wine types and a range of styles.

penalty_signals.signal: Declaring in the introduction that only one of the two named varieties will be covered
penalty_signals.quote: It is sometimes said that the candidate has the right to control the content of the essay, but when the question specifies the varietal commentary required, it is not sufficient for a candidate to state in their introduction that they do not intend to address one or other of the named varieties.

penalty_signals.signal: An 'all I know about oak' brain-dump untethered from the two varieties
penalty_signals.quote: Examiners also commented that the responses were too frequently a dump of 'all I know about oak' without giving particular reference to Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon.

penalty_signals.signal: Premium-end bias
penalty_signals.quote: Again, Examiners noted that candidates focussed too heavily on the premium end of the market.

examples_expected.specificity: Global, spanning classic and non-classic origins for both varieties and a range of price points; per the Panel Chair, "Examples should be used to support arguments/statements rather than as statements of fact. Examples should also be global and cover all wine types where appropriate."
examples_expected.quote: Candidates must be able to show depth and breadth of knowledge about which styles and qualities are produced from these two varieties globally and consider styles with reference to classic / non classic origins.

scope_traps.trap: Treating the question as being about oak barrels alone
scope_traps.quote: the responses were too frequently a dump of 'all I know about oak' without giving particular reference to Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon.

scope_traps.trap: Answering on one named variety only
scope_traps.quote: Many candidates asserted their right to speak only of either Chardonnay or Cabernet Sauvignon and consequently limited their scope for gaining marks.

performance_note: "This question was generally better answered than most others."
extraction_notes: The commentary names no specific producers or regions for this question, so named_in_report is empty; the requirement for global/classic-vs-non-classic breadth is stated abstractly. The examples_expected specificity field draws partly on the Paper 2 preamble (Meg Brodtmann MW), which is paper-wide evidence.

question_text: How can a wine's tannin profile be managed during vinification?
command_word_demand: The examiners emphasise the scope-limiting phrase in the stem and the need to convert technical detail into argument: "The question clearly states "during vinification" so candidates should limit themselves to the winemaking process." And: "The less successful scripts tended to either offer 'all I know about tannin', in rather chatty style, or provided a lot of technical detail about the subject but were unable to interpret that detail into a sensible argument."

required_elements.element: Stay within vinification — viticulture/harvest gets a brief mention at most
required_elements.quote: The question clearly states "during vinification" so candidates should limit themselves to the winemaking process. A brief mention of harvesting grapes at optimum phenolic ripeness is fine but candidates must focus on the winemaking.

required_elements.element: Demonstrate the tannin extraction processes and the aids used to extract, add and/or fix tannins, plus oak tannins
required_elements.quote: Candidates must demonstrate an understanding of the tannin extraction processes, the use of aids to extract, add and / or fix tannins and the use of oak tannins.

required_elements.element: Focus on red winemaking while noting white, sparkling, sweet and fortified where relevant
required_elements.quote: Mention could be made of white, sparkling, sweet and fortified wine but should focus on red winemaking.

required_elements.element: Clear command of cap management techniques — how they differ and why each is used
required_elements.quote: In relation to the extraction process, candidates should have a clear understanding of the various cap management techniques, how they differ and why they are used.

required_elements.element: Cover post-fermentation operations: post-ferment maceration, microoxygenation, barrel ageing
required_elements.quote: They should have also included some discussion of post fermentation maceration and other post fermentation operations that can manage tannin (ie microoxygenation, ageing in barrels, etc).

required_elements.element: Explain pressing with authority — press fractions and fining of press fractions and free run
required_elements.quote: For those that covered pressing, few really explained with any level of authority the way tannin can be managed in a press through fractions - fining pressing fractions (and free run) is an important way of managing tannin.

required_elements.element: Address entry-level as well as premium wine
required_elements.quote: Candidates must not just focus on the premium end of the market - it could be argued that judicial tannin management is more important at "entry level" - pressing off skins before the end of primary fermentation is common practice.

required_elements.element: Structure the answer as a logical flow through the winemaking process, opened by a solid introduction
required_elements.quote: With these types of questions a logical flow to the answer helps immensely. As winemaking is itself a flow from one activity to another, it makes sense that answers cover the winemaking process in a coherent way. A solid introduction alluding to the points that will be discussed is important.

required_elements.element: Include oenological tannins — colour stabilisation, structural improvement of early-pressed wines
required_elements.quote: Many candidates, even the better ones, tended to overlook the use of oenological tannins in winemaking. Points raised could have been in connection with stabilising the colour with tannin or improving structural elements of early-pressed wines.

required_elements.element: Microoxygenation may be discussed
required_elements.quote: Candidates could also discuss microoxygenation.

credit_signals.signal: A coherent chronological flow through the winemaking process, signposted by the introduction
credit_signals.quote: With these types of questions a logical flow to the answer helps immensely… A solid introduction alluding to the points that will be discussed is important.

penalty_signals.signal: 'All I know about tannin' in a chatty register
penalty_signals.quote: The less successful scripts tended to either offer 'all I know about tannin', in rather chatty style…

penalty_signals.signal: Technical detail that is never converted into an argument
penalty_signals.quote: or provided a lot of technical detail about the subject but were unable to interpret that detail into a sensible argument.

penalty_signals.signal: Over-weighting fermentation and leaving the rest of the process thin
penalty_signals.quote: Many candidates tended to focus too much on fermentation and not give a full answer.

penalty_signals.signal: Overlooking oenological tannins
penalty_signals.quote: Many candidates, even the better ones, tended to overlook the use of oenological tannins in winemaking.

penalty_signals.signal: Disparaging particular winemaking methods
penalty_signals.quote: Lastly, as a caution, be very wary of making derogatory remarks about certain winemaking methods (i.e. rotary fermenters). These comments can show a lack of understanding of the wine industry as a whole and can 'make the Examiners blood heat up!' (to quote one Examiner).

penalty_signals.signal: Premium-only framing
penalty_signals.quote: Candidates must not just focus on the premium end of the market…

examples_expected.specificity: The question-specific commentary sets no example granularity; the Paper 2 preamble governs — examples must support the argument, be global, and cover all wine types where appropriate.
examples_expected.quote: Examples should be used to support arguments/statements rather than as statements of fact. Examples should also be global and cover all wine types where appropriate.

scope_traps.trap: Drifting into viticulture and harvest decisions rather than vinification
scope_traps.quote: The question clearly states "during vinification" so candidates should limit themselves to the winemaking process. A brief mention of harvesting grapes at optimum phenolic ripeness is fine but candidates must focus on the winemaking.

scope_traps.trap: Treating tannin management as a premium-wine concern only
scope_traps.quote: it could be argued that judicial tannin management is more important at "entry level" - pressing off skins before the end of primary fermentation is common practice.

performance_note: "This question had the highest pass rate in the Paper."
extraction_notes: examples_expected.quote is taken from the Paper 2 preamble, not from this question's own commentary, because the question-specific commentary does not discuss examples — a grader should weight the example requirement here as paper-wide rather than question-specific.

question_text: Discuss the impact of malolactic fermentation, or its absence, on wine style.
command_word_demand: "This question is looking for the candidate to give a concise definition of what malolactic fermentation is and does, and then apply this to a number of wine styles outlining the relevant impact that MLF has on that style." The examiners stress this needed planning, not the default Paper 2 process narrative: "this question required more than the winemaking flow-chart approach which can be used on so many Paper 2 answers."

definitions_required.quote: This question is looking for the candidate to give a concise definition of what malolactic fermentation is and does, and then apply this to a number of wine styles…

definitions_required.term: the bacteria responsible for MLF (Oenococcus oeni)
definitions_required.quote: The main cause of concern was a failure to define clearly the bacteria responsible for malolactic fermentation.

required_elements.element: Give a concise, watertight definition of MLF and what it does, up front
required_elements.quote: With this in mind, students were likely to run into trouble later in the paper if their introduction wasn't watertight.

required_elements.element: Name the bacteria correctly and currently — Oenococcus oeni, not Leuconostoc oenos — and know it occurs naturally
required_elements.quote: It was previously called Leuconostoc oenos but the name was changed in the late 1990's and therefore scripts should be clear in referencing the current name… In addition several students seem convinced that Oenococcus oeni doesn't occur naturally - perhaps due to the fact that winemakers do add it as a cultured bacterium.

required_elements.element: Demonstrate the full process — bacteria involved, fermentation temperature, possible risks — and tie each to style impact
required_elements.quote: Candidates must demonstrate a thorough understanding of the MLF process - bacteria involved, fermentation temperature, possible risks - and discuss this in relation to the impact on wine style (acid reduction, bi-products of the MLF).

required_elements.element: Apply MLF across styles with examples — sparkling, white, red and possibly fortified
required_elements.quote: It is important to give examples across styles from sparkling, white, red and possibly fortified to substantiate the argument.

required_elements.element: Discuss red wine properly, including reds that do NOT undergo MLF
required_elements.quote: Too many candidates simply dismissed the impact of MLF on red wine as 'all red wines go through MLF'… the impact of MLF on red wines as well as reds that don't go through MLF could have had a paragraph of discussion. Apart from Nouveau styles, there are a number of sweet red wines on the market now that do not undergo MLF.

required_elements.element: Get the basic science right — direction of pH change, realistic MLF temperatures
required_elements.quote: The main issue however seemed to be technical misunderstandings. Not only were the bacteria involved a confusion for candidates but also the basic science of MLF. pH levels were all over the place and either rose or fell after MLF. Ideal temperatures to conduct MLF also varied from ''low 12ºC'' to "high 36ºC".

required_elements.element: Structure by wine category plus non-style impacts
required_elements.quote: The best looked to break it down into red wines, white wines/sparkling bases and other impacts such as microbiological.

credit_signals.signal: A planned structure splitting reds / whites and sparkling bases / other impacts such as microbiological
credit_signals.quote: It also required careful planning - this question required more than the winemaking flow-chart approach which can be used on so many Paper 2 answers. The best looked to break it down into red wines, white wines/sparkling bases and other impacts such as microbiological.

credit_signals.signal: Recognising where the marks actually lay — whites and sparkling
credit_signals.quote: Clearly, there were more marks to be gained in considering the impacts on white and sparkling wines…

penalty_signals.signal: Failing to define the bacteria responsible, or using the superseded name
penalty_signals.quote: The main cause of concern was a failure to define clearly the bacteria responsible for malolactic fermentation. Students need to update their knowledge of LAB strains.

penalty_signals.signal: Claiming Oenococcus oeni does not occur naturally
penalty_signals.quote: In addition several students seem convinced that Oenococcus oeni doesn't occur naturally…

penalty_signals.signal: Dismissing reds with 'all red wines go through MLF'
penalty_signals.quote: Too many candidates simply dismissed the impact of MLF on red wine as 'all red wines go through MLF'.

penalty_signals.signal: Answering almost entirely on Chardonnay
penalty_signals.quote: More importantly a number of candidates attempted the question centred almost exclusively on the impact of MLF on Chardonnay with a brief mention of aromatic white wines and thus didn't answer the question with sufficient breadth.

penalty_signals.signal: Wrong or inconsistent technical facts on pH movement and MLF temperature
penalty_signals.quote: pH levels were all over the place and either rose or fell after MLF. Ideal temperatures to conduct MLF also varied from ''low 12ºC'' to "high 36ºC".

penalty_signals.signal: Defaulting to the winemaking flow-chart template
penalty_signals.quote: this question required more than the winemaking flow-chart approach which can be used on so many Paper 2 answers.

examples_expected.specificity: Spread across sparkling, white, red and possibly fortified — breadth of style, not depth on one variety.
named_in_report: sweet red wines on the market now that do not undergo MLF
examples_expected.quote: It is important to give examples across styles from sparkling, white, red and possibly fortified to substantiate the argument.

scope_traps.trap: Reading the question as being about Chardonnay
scope_traps.quote: a number of candidates attempted the question centred almost exclusively on the impact of MLF on Chardonnay with a brief mention of aromatic white wines and thus didn't answer the question with sufficient breadth.

scope_traps.trap: Ignoring the 'or its absence' half of the stem
scope_traps.quote: the impact of MLF on red wines as well as reds that don't go through MLF could have had a paragraph of discussion.

performance_note: "Perhaps because this question seemed fairly straightforward at first glance, a great many candidates chose it. Only one really gave an excellent and comprehensive answer along with a few passable ones. The rest seemed to struggle."
extraction_notes: The report itself supplies substantive technical content on Oenococcus oeni (acid tolerance, 10% ethanol tolerance, the Leuconostoc oenos renaming) — this is examiner text, not extractor knowledge, and is quoted as such. Note the doubled apostrophes in ''low 12ºC'' are as printed in the source.

question_text: What are the winemaker's options and challenges in colour management for different wine styles?
command_word: What are the winemaker's options and challenges
command_word_demand: A two-part stem, and the examiners marked papers down for answering only the first: "a number of candidates simply described the practices in obtaining colour, answering the first part of the question only." Breadth with restraint was the demand: "With such large questions it's critical to have a light touch with each area of the answer, not to get bogged down in overly detailed description of what one particular winemaker does as an example."

required_elements.element: Answer both parts — options AND challenges
required_elements.quote: Most candidates seemed comfortable covering colour extraction techniques in different winemaking styles, but a number of candidates simply described the practices in obtaining colour, answering the first part of the question only.

required_elements.element: Establish the core relationship between colour and skins across a wide variety of process options
required_elements.quote: A broad essay inviting the candidate to demonstrate their knowledge of a wide variety of process options and the core relationship between colour and skins.

required_elements.element: Treat the inter-related questions of tannin management, pH and wine stability
required_elements.quote: The inter-related notions of tannin management and also pH and wine stability are critical.

required_elements.element: Address spoilage: rot-related colour destabilization and oxidation, deliberate or accidental, post fermentation
required_elements.quote: Spoilage factors from rot- related colour destabilization through to oxidation - deliberate or accidental - post fermentation should also have been addressed.

required_elements.element: Cover post-fermentation processes, additions (tannin, colour, enzymes, oak), fining and the role of oxygen
required_elements.quote: Candidates also often failed to mention, or showed poor understanding of, winemaking processes post-fermentation, additions (tannin, colour, enzymes, oak) and fining, as well as the role of oxygen. The best answers covered at least a few of these areas, giving a much more complete answer to the question.

required_elements.element: Open with a clear, well-structured introduction that maps the answer
required_elements.quote: As with all large, open questions where there is the temptation to write too much, a good, clear introduction is necessary. A well-structured introduction lays out the map for answering the question - candidates who have one generally stand a good chance of passing.

required_elements.element: Give specific, factual detail rather than vague comparatives
required_elements.quote: Others used statements like "high temperatures" and "longer time" - more specific, factual insight was required.

credit_signals.signal: Using the chronology of the winemaking process as the structural spine
credit_signals.quote: Paper 2 answers generally benefit from using the natural structure and chronology of the winemaking process as a basis for their structure - for the Examiner it is logical and easy to follow and shows an organised pattern of thinking. It also helps the candidate identify areas of interest that might easily be forgotten under the pressure of the Exam.

credit_signals.signal: Covering at least several of the neglected post-fermentation areas
credit_signals.quote: The best answers covered at least a few of these areas, giving a much more complete answer to the question.

credit_signals.signal: Good tempo and logical flow, with technical assumptions never in doubt
credit_signals.quote: Passing answers normally have a good tempo and a logical flow - and the Examiner should of course never be questioning a candidate's technical knowledge or assumptions about winemaking practices.

penalty_signals.signal: Describing colour extraction only — first half of the question answered
penalty_signals.quote: a number of candidates simply described the practices in obtaining colour, answering the first part of the question only.

penalty_signals.signal: Vague, unquantified statements
penalty_signals.quote: Others used statements like "high temperatures" and "longer time" - more specific, factual insight was required.

penalty_signals.signal: Silence on, or poor understanding of, post-fermentation processes, additions, fining and oxygen
penalty_signals.quote: Candidates also often failed to mention, or showed poor understanding of, winemaking processes post-fermentation, additions (tannin, colour, enzymes, oak) and fining, as well as the role of oxygen.

penalty_signals.signal: Getting bogged down in one winemaker's practice at the expense of coverage
penalty_signals.quote: With such large questions it's critical to have a light touch with each area of the answer, not to get bogged down in overly detailed description of what one particular winemaker does as an example.

examples_expected.specificity: Used with a light touch to illustrate a point — the report explicitly warns against extended description of a single producer's practice. The Paper 2 preamble adds that examples should be global, cover all wine types where appropriate, and support arguments rather than stand as statements of fact.
examples_expected.quote: With such large questions it's critical to have a light touch with each area of the answer, not to get bogged down in overly detailed description of what one particular winemaker does as an example.

scope_traps.trap: Treating the question as colour extraction (i.e. red winemaking) only, rather than colour management across different wine styles
scope_traps.quote: Most candidates seemed comfortable covering colour extraction techniques in different winemaking styles, but a number of candidates simply described the practices in obtaining colour, answering the first part of the question only.

performance_note: "Despite being a large topic area with many different areas to address, this should have been a relatively straightforward question to approach." No attempt or pass rate is stated for this question.
extraction_notes: A large share of this commentary is Paper 2-wide essay craft advice (introductions, chronological structure, tempo) that the Panel Chair applies generically; it has been recorded but a grader should not treat structure alone as the discriminator. A page number ('the natural structure and 12 chronology') was removed from one quote.

question_text: Examine the pros and cons of skin contact during the winemaking process.
command_word_demand: The examiners want a declared method of attack and genuine analysis, not enumeration: "Although the question seems straightforward, it is very important to clarify how it will be approached… The question can thus be approached either through each category of wine or by the various outcomes that will be affected by skin contact." And: "Time and again the one thing that appears lacking is evidence of original thinking, or critical analysis."

definitions_required.quote: Candidates must provide a useful definition of skin contact and should make it clear that this relates to red, white and rosé wines and can be applied to all wine styles (table, sparkling and fortified).

required_elements.element: Provide a useful definition of skin contact
required_elements.quote: Candidates must provide a useful definition of skin contact…

required_elements.element: Cover red, white and rosé, and all wine styles — table, sparkling and fortified
required_elements.quote: should make it clear that this relates to red, white and rosé wines and can be applied to all wine styles (table, sparkling and fortified).

required_elements.element: Do not exclude red winemaking on the grounds that all reds have skin contact
required_elements.quote: While it can be useful to clearly state the areas you will address in your answer it is not acceptable to state that you will omit areas like red winemaking because all red wines have skin contact.

required_elements.element: Show good understanding of the processes for each wine colour and style, supported by examples from around the world
required_elements.quote: Candidates should demonstrate a good understanding of the processes involved with each wine colour and style and use examples from around the world to support their statements.

required_elements.element: Choose and declare a coherent approach — by wine category or by outcome
required_elements.quote: The question can thus be approached either through each category of wine or by the various outcomes that will be affected by skin contact.

required_elements.element: Cover both sides: the range of skin contact methods AND their risks
required_elements.quote: Such answers showed understanding as well as knowledge, covering a range of skin contact methods and their risks.

required_elements.element: Reach summary-level concepts — e.g. that all wines have some element of skin contact, or the ten-year trend to more extraction on whites and less on reds
required_elements.quote: Good (but all too few) answers to this question broached summary concepts, for instance that all wines experience an element of skin contact, or that there has been a trend in the past 10 years to aim for more extraction on whites and less extraction on reds.

required_elements.element: Use examples to show multiple routes to one outcome, or one technique serving different outcomes
required_elements.quote: Few candidates are able to present examples in a way that shows there are different ways to the same solution (e.g. winemaker 1 does A to arrive at C, while winemaker 2 does B to arrive at C) or that one can use the same techniques to arrive at different outcomes (e.g. winemaker 1 punches down because they like gentle tannin extraction, while winemaker 2 punches down to achieve full extraction).

credit_signals.signal: Demonstrating that the wine world is complex, local and global at once, and changing
credit_signals.quote: In this way the candidate can demonstrate that the world of wine is complex and subjective, highly localised and global, and ever changing - and that they understand it.

credit_signals.signal: Detailed but economical prose
credit_signals.quote: Good, passing answers are detailed but do not waste words or repeat them.

credit_signals.signal: Broaching summary concepts and trends rather than only mechanisms
credit_signals.quote: Good (but all too few) answers to this question broached summary concepts, for instance that all wines experience an element of skin contact, or that there has been a trend in the past 10 years to aim for more extraction on whites and less extraction on reds.

penalty_signals.signal: Poor structure or an incomplete answer that omits major winemaking styles
penalty_signals.quote: As per the previous question, failure often resulted because of poor structure or incomplete answers that failed to address major winemaking styles (red, rosé, white etc).

penalty_signals.signal: Listing everything known about the topic as a substitute for an answer
penalty_signals.quote: There is definitely a trend for candidates to list all they know about a topic area as a form of answer - this will rarely pass, or producing a load of examples with no context or argument linking them.

penalty_signals.signal: An introduction that only announces the essay and restates the question
penalty_signals.quote: A number of introductions end with sentences like, 'This essay will examine…' and then repeat the question, failing to refer the Examiner to what the candidate intends to write and conveys a lack of mastery or flow on the topic.

penalty_signals.signal: Announcing that red winemaking will be skipped
penalty_signals.quote: it is not acceptable to state that you will omit areas like red winemaking because all red wines have skin contact.

examples_expected.specificity: Global, and deployed comparatively — showing different routes to the same outcome, or the same technique serving different outcomes — rather than listed without context.
examples_expected.quote: Candidates should demonstrate a good understanding of the processes involved with each wine colour and style and use examples from around the world to support their statements.

scope_traps.trap: Narrowing the question to white/orange 'skin contact' wines and skipping red and rosé
scope_traps.quote: should make it clear that this relates to red, white and rosé wines and can be applied to all wine styles (table, sparkling and fortified).

performance_note: "A similar style question to the previous one, answered perhaps slightly better with a handful of good passes. Also quite similar to a question from last year's Exam so perhaps candidates were well prepared for this very topical area."
extraction_notes: The commentary names no producers, regions or wines, so named_in_report is empty despite examples being explicitly required. The 'winemaker 1 / winemaker 2' passage is an examiner illustration of METHOD, not a factual example to be reproduced.
